name: Atlantis (legend)
dateLabel: Plato (c. 360 BCE) set it c. 9600 BCE
evidenceNote: Not proven: no archaeological evidence has been found. Atlantis comes only from two dialogues written by the philosopher Plato, and classicists agree it is a made-up story.
summary: Atlantis is the island empire in Plato's dialogues Timaeus and Critias, written around 360 BCE. Plato says it lay 'beyond the Pillars of Heracles' (the Strait of Gibraltar) and sank 9,000 years before the time of the Athenian lawmaker Solon, after losing a war against an idealised early Athens. Scholars read it as a moral tale about pride and power. Some suggest Plato borrowed ideas from real events such as the Thera eruption, but no ruins have ever been found. The point here only marks where Plato placed it.

name: Lepenski Vir
evidenceNote: No writing existed; its story comes from excavations begun in the 1960s and from radiocarbon dates, which still leave the start date uncertain.
summary: Lepenski Vir sits on the Danube in the Iron Gates gorge of Serbia. Fishers and hunters lived here for thousands of years. Between about 6300 and 6000 BCE, as the first farmers arrived in the region, they built unusual trapezoid-shaped houses with red lime-plaster floors and carved large boulder sculptures of fish-like human faces. Because the village was planned and lived in all year, some have called it Europe's 'first city', though it was a village of foragers. The remains were moved uphill when a dam flooded the gorge and are shown under a roof.

image.caption: House floors of Lepenski Vir under the protective roof

name: Star Carr
evidenceNote: No writing existed; radiocarbon dates from finds preserved in waterlogged peat show people used the lakeside for about 800 years.
summary: Star Carr in North Yorkshire is the most informative Middle Stone Age (Mesolithic) site in Britain. Hunter-gatherers camped on the shore of a lake soon after the Ice Age, when Britain was still joined to mainland Europe. Because the site lies in wet peat, wood, bone and antler survived. Finds include Britain's oldest known structure, 21 red-deer skull caps that may have been worn as headdresses, and nearly 200 antler points. Radiocarbon dates place the activity between about 9300 and 8500 BCE.

name: Sesklo
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the dates come from excavated layers and radiocarbon, and the oldest pre-pottery levels are still debated.
summary: Sesklo, near Volos in Thessaly, gave its name to one of Europe's earliest farming cultures. Its people grew wheat and barley and herded sheep, goats, cattle and pigs. The oldest levels have no pottery, but villagers soon made fine painted ware with red and brown geometric patterns. Houses of mudbrick on stone foundations were laid out with some planning, and a few had two floors. At its peak, around 5000 BCE, the settlement may have covered about 20 hectares, though population estimates of up to 5,000 people are uncertain.

name: Starčevo
evidenceNote: No writing existed; dates come from radiocarbon results at many Starčevo-culture villages, not just this one.
summary: The village of Starčevo, on the north bank of the Danube opposite Belgrade, is the type site of the Starčevo culture: the first farmers of the central Balkans. These communities came north from Greece and Anatolia, bringing wheat, barley, domestic animals and pottery. They lived in small villages of pit-houses and timber houses along the rivers. Radiocarbon dates from 2020 suggest farming spread up the river valleys of Serbia from about 6200 BCE. Their descendants helped carry farming on into central Europe.

name: Vinča–Belo Brdo
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the Vinča symbols scratched on pots are not considered true writing by most scholars, so dates come from layers and radiocarbon.
summary: Belo Brdo ('White Hill') at Vinča, 14 km downstream from Belgrade, is a tell: a mound about 10 metres high made almost entirely of the remains of settlements built one on top of another. Its main layers belong to the Vinča culture, which is named after it. Vinča farmers made thousands of clay figurines and scratched mysterious signs on pottery, and the culture has some of the earliest known evidence of copper smelting. Excavations began in 1908, and finds are now in museums in Belgrade, Oxford and London.

name: Cairn of Barnenez
dateLabel: built c. 4850–4000 BCE; reused in the 3rd millennium BCE
evidenceNote: No writing existed; radiocarbon dating shows the two building phases.
summary: The Cairn of Barnenez in northern Brittany is a long stone mound containing a row of passage-grave chambers; a second phase added six more. Radiocarbon dates put its first phase between about 4850 and 4250 BCE and its second between 4450 and 4000 BCE, making it one of the oldest megalithic monuments in Europe. Some stones are carved with symbols. Pottery shows people reused it in the Bronze Age. In the 1950s part of it was being quarried for paving stone before it was saved and restored.

name: Varna Necropolis
evidenceNote: No writing existed; radiocarbon dates published in 2006 show when the graves were dug.
summary: This Copper Age cemetery was found by accident in 1972 by an excavator driver in Varna, Bulgaria. Archaeologists have uncovered 294 graves, some filled with gold ornaments, copper tools, fine flint blades and shells. It holds the oldest large hoard of worked gold in the world. The richest grave, of a man buried with gold regalia, is the oldest known burial of an elite person: an early sign that some people had far more wealth and status than others. Several 'symbolic' graves held no body, only objects and clay masks.

image.caption: A grave from the Varna necropolis with gold ornaments, Varna Archaeological Museum

name: Akrotiri
dateLabel: settled by c. 4500 BCE; buried c. 1600 BCE
evidenceNote: A few Linear A signs survive, but that script is undeciphered, so we rely on excavation; the eruption is dated by radiocarbon to about 1620–1530 BCE, and archaeologists debate the exact date.
summary: Akrotiri on the island of Santorini (Thera) was a busy Bronze Age harbour town with paved streets, drains and houses up to three storeys high. It traded across the Aegean and was closely linked to Minoan Crete. In the 16th century BCE a huge volcanic eruption buried it in ash, preserving it like a Bronze Age Pompeii, with beautiful wall paintings, pottery and furniture. Its ancient name is unknown. Excavation began in 1967, and a roof now covers the ruins.

image.caption: Excavated houses at Akrotiri under the modern roof

name: Carnac stones
evidenceNote: No writing existed; dates come from excavation of the stones and nearby tombs, and exactly when each row was raised is uncertain.
summary: Around Carnac in southern Brittany more than 3,000 standing stones, cut from local granite, stand in long rows, together with stone tombs and burial mounds. It is the largest collection of its kind in the world. They were raised by Stone Age farmers, perhaps from around 4500 BCE, with most work probably around 3300 BCE. Nobody knows for sure what the rows were for. Local legends later said they were Roman soldiers turned to stone.

image.caption: Standing stones of the Le Ménec alignments, Carnac

name: Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum
evidenceNote: No writing existed; dating comes from pottery styles and excavated layers.
summary: The Hypogeum ('underground place') at Paola, Malta, is a maze of chambers cut into solid rock, covering about 500 square metres. It was used as a sanctuary and burial place, and the remains of more than 7,000 people were recorded. Finds included finely decorated pottery and stone and clay figures. Builders found it by accident in 1902 while cutting water cisterns. It is one of the best-preserved works of Malta's temple-building culture.

name: Talianki mega-site
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the town was found from the air in the 1970s and dated by excavation, and its population is only an estimate that scholars disagree about.
summary: Near the village of Talianky in central Ukraine lies the largest known settlement of Neolithic Europe, built by the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture. Rings of joined houses, many with two storeys and painted walls, spread over 3 to 4.5 square kilometres of plateau. Estimates of its population range from about 6,000 to more than 15,000 people, which would make it as big as early cities in Mesopotamia. Trypillian settlements usually lasted only 60 to 80 years before their houses were burned, for reasons scholars still debate.

name: Dolmen of Menga
evidenceNote: No writing existed; its age comes from excavation and dating of the site.
summary: The Dolmen of Menga near Antequera in southern Spain is one of the largest stone tombs in Europe. Builders used 32 huge stone blocks, the biggest weighing about 180 tonnes, to make a long chamber, then covered it with earth to form a hill. When it was opened in the 19th century, it held the skeletons of several hundred people. Unusually, its entrance faces a nearby mountain, the Peña de los Enamorados, rather than the sunrise. It is part of the Antequera Dolmens World Heritage Site.

name: Ġgantija temples
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the temples are dated by pottery phases and radiocarbon.
summary: Ġgantija, on the island of Gozo, is the oldest of the Megalithic Temples of Malta. Its two temples, built around 3600 BCE from enormous limestone blocks, are older than Egypt's pyramids and among the oldest free-standing stone buildings in the world. Their name means 'place of giants', from a local legend that a giantess built them. Figurines found inside suggest religious rituals. Malta's temple-building culture ended around 2500 BCE.

image.caption: The Ġgantija temples on the Xagħra plateau, Gozo

name: Ness of Brodgar
evidenceNote: No writing existed; excavations from 2003 to 2024 and radiocarbon dates tell its story.
summary: The Ness of Brodgar is a complex of large stone buildings on a strip of land between the Ring of Brodgar and the Stones of Stenness in Orkney, Scotland. Excavators found massive walls, decorated stone slabs and a large building described as a Neolithic temple. People gathered here for well over a thousand years, and by about 2200 BCE the site had been closed and partly taken apart. After excavation ended in 2024, it was covered over again to protect it.

name: Ötzi the Iceman (find site)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; his body and equipment have been studied scientifically since 1991.
summary: In 1991 two hikers found a man's body coming out of the ice near the Tisenjoch pass, 3,210 metres up in the Alps on the Austria–Italy border. Ötzi lived more than 5,300 years ago and is Europe's oldest known natural mummy. He carried a copper axe, a flint knife, a longbow and a quiver of arrows, and wore leather clothes and a bearskin cap. An arrowhead in his shoulder shows that he was killed by another person. His body is now kept at the South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology in Bolzano.

sources.title: South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology: Ötzi the Iceman

name: Skara Brae
evidenceNote: No writing existed; radiocarbon dates and excavation tell us when people lived here.
summary: Skara Brae, on the west coast of Orkney's Mainland, is Europe's most complete Neolithic village. A storm in 1850 uncovered stone houses buried in sand dunes. Each house was a single room joined to the others by covered passages and had built-in stone furniture: a 'dresser', box beds and a central hearth. Farmers lived here from about 3180 to 2500 BCE. No one knows why the village was abandoned: some think sand buried it, others that people left gradually. It is part of the Heart of Neolithic Orkney World Heritage Site.

image.caption: A house with stone furniture at Skara Brae

sources.title: Historic Environment Scotland: Skara Brae, history

name: Newgrange
dateLabel: built c. 3100 BCE; out of use by the Bronze Age
evidenceNote: No writing existed; radiocarbon dates from the building and excavations from 1962 to 1975 tell us its age.
summary: Newgrange in County Meath, Ireland, is a huge passage tomb built around 3100 BCE, older than Stonehenge and the pyramids of Giza. A stone passage leads into a cross-shaped chamber inside a round mound ringed by carved kerbstones. At sunrise on the winter solstice, light shines through a 'roof-box' over the entrance and fills the chamber. Burnt and unburnt human bones were found inside. By the start of the Bronze Age it was falling into ruin. It is the main monument of the Brú na Bóinne World Heritage Site.

image.caption: The restored white quartz front of Newgrange

name: Stonehenge
evidenceNote: No writing existed; radiocarbon dating of antler picks, bones and pits shows its building phases, but its purpose is still debated.
summary: Stonehenge on Salisbury Plain in England was built in stages from about 3100 to 1600 BCE. It began as a circular ditch and bank. The great ring of sarsen stones, each about 25 tonnes and topped by lintels joined with woodworking-style joints, was put up between about 2600 and 2400 BCE. Smaller bluestones were brought from Wales. The monument lines up with sunrise at the summer solstice and sunset at the winter solstice, and hundreds of burial mounds surround it.

name: Los Millares
evidenceNote: No writing existed; radiocarbon dates and excavations since the 1890s tell its story.
summary: Los Millares, near Almería in southern Spain, was a fortified Copper Age town of perhaps 1,000 people. Three rings of stone walls with bastions protected it, and four small forts guarded the approach. Inside were simple houses and a workshop for smelting copper. Outside lay a cemetery of about 80 passage-grave tombs. It was found in 1891 during railway building and first dug by Luis Siret. It is the type site of the Los Millares culture.

name: El Argar
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the dates come from graves and layers excavated since the 1880s.
summary: El Argar, on a flat hilltop near Antas in Almería, southeastern Spain, is the type site of the Early Bronze Age Argaric culture. Behind a wall stood rows of long rectangular houses, and more than a thousand graves were dug inside the houses themselves, many with bronze daggers, axes and ornaments. The Argaric people were among the first in Iberia to use bronze widely, and some archaeologists think their society was ruled like an early state.

name: Knossos (Palace of Minos)
dateLabel: palace c. 1900–1350 BCE (hill settled from c. 7000 BCE)
evidenceNote: Late clay tablets in Linear B (early Greek) name Knossos as Ko-no-so, but the Minoans' own Linear A script is undeciphered, so most of its history comes from excavation.
summary: Knossos, just south of Heraklion on Crete, was the largest centre of the Minoan civilisation. People settled the hill around 7000 BCE. The first palace, built around 1900 BCE, was rebuilt after a destruction around 1700 BCE into a huge complex of courtyards, storerooms, shrines and painted halls. It was probably a centre of government, trade and religion. Thousands of Linear B tablets were found there. Arthur Evans dug it from 1900 and rebuilt parts in concrete, which still shapes how visitors see it.

name: Su Nuraxi di Barumini
dateLabel: tower 17th–13th century BCE; village to the 6th century BCE
evidenceNote: The Nuragic people left no writing; dates come from excavations begun in the 1950s and radiocarbon.
summary: Su Nuraxi ('the nuraghe') at Barumini is the finest example of Sardinia's nuraghi: stone towers built by the Nuragic civilisation. Its central basalt tower, with three chambers stacked inside, rose about 18.6 metres. Later four corner towers and a curtain wall were added around it, and a village of round stone huts grew outside from the 13th to the 6th century BCE. Archaeologists still debate whether nuraghi were mainly fortresses, homes of leaders or religious buildings. Giovanni Lilliu excavated it in the 1950s.

image.caption: The nuraghe of Su Nuraxi at Barumini

name: Mycenae
dateLabel: citadel c. 1600–1100 BCE (Lion Gate c. 1250 BCE)
evidenceNote: Linear B clay tablets in early Greek were found here, and later Greek writers describe it; Homer's King Agamemnon, though, belongs to legend.
summary: Mycenae, on a hill in the Argolid, gave its name to the Mycenaean civilisation of Bronze Age Greece. Rich shaft graves full of gold date from around 1600 BCE. Around 1250 BCE its walls of giant 'Cyclopean' blocks were extended and the Lion Gate built, crowned by two carved lions or lionesses. The Treasury of Atreus is a vast beehive-shaped tomb. Mycenae was destroyed in the Bronze Age collapse around 1200 BCE and survived only as a small town until 468 BCE.

image.caption: The path up to the Lion Gate, Mycenae

name: Nebra sky disc find site (Mittelberg)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the disc was dug up illegally in 1999, so its date rests on scientific tests and the objects buried with it; most experts accept a Bronze Age date, though a 2020 paper argued for a later one.
summary: In 1999 treasure hunters with a metal detector illegally dug up a bronze disc on the Mittelberg hill near Nebra, Germany. The state archaeologist recovered it in a police sting in 2002. The disc, inlaid with gold, shows the Sun or full Moon, a crescent Moon and stars, including a cluster thought to be the Pleiades. It is the oldest known concrete picture of the sky, buried around 1600 BCE by people of the Únětice culture. It is now in the State Museum of Prehistory in Halle and on UNESCO's Memory of the World register.

sources.title: State Museum of Prehistory Halle: Nebra Sky Disc

name: Hallstatt salt mines and cemetery
evidenceNote: No writing existed here; the story comes from more than a thousand excavated graves and finds in the salt mines.
summary: High above the lake town of Hallstatt in Austria, people mined rock salt from the Bronze Age onward. Salt was precious for preserving food, and the trade made the community rich. From 1846 Johann Georg Ramsauer excavated a huge prehistoric cemetery here, with more than a thousand burials, many rich in bronze and iron objects. These finds were so important that the whole Early Iron Age culture of central Europe is named after Hallstatt. A great landslide in the mid-4th century BCE ended the ancient mining.

name: Olympia
evidenceNote: Greek inscriptions, victor lists and writers record the sanctuary and its Games, alongside excavations since the 1870s.
summary: Olympia, in the western Peloponnese, was a great sanctuary of the god Zeus and the home of the ancient Olympic Games. By tradition the first Games were held in 776 BCE, and they took place every four years for more than a thousand years. Athletes from all over the Greek world competed, which helped Greeks feel they were one people. The site had temples, treasuries, a stadium and training grounds. The Games ended in the 390s CE under the Christian emperor Theodosius I and later inspired the modern Olympic Games.

name: Biskupin
dateLabel: built c. 747–722 BCE; lived in into the 6th century BCE
evidenceNote: No writing existed; tree rings in the oak timbers show when the trees were cut, and radiocarbon dates the later use.
summary: Biskupin in north-central Poland was a fortified wooden town on a marshy island, built by people of the Lusatian culture. Tree-ring dating shows its oak logs were felled between 747 and 722 BCE. About a hundred log houses of the same size and plan stood in neat rows along streets paved with planks, all inside a timber rampart. A schoolteacher and his pupils found it in 1933. Parts of the town have been rebuilt as an open-air museum.

image.caption: Reconstructed gate and rampart at Biskupin

name: Heuneburg
evidenceNote: The Celts here left no writing; excavation tells its story, and the idea that it was the town of Pyrene mentioned by the Greek writer Herodotus is only a possibility.
summary: The Heuneburg is a hillfort above the Danube in southern Germany and one of the most important early Celtic centres of the Hallstatt period. Around 600 BCE its builders replaced a timber wall with a whitewashed mudbrick wall on stone foundations, a Mediterranean technique unknown elsewhere north of the Alps. Valuable imported goods show trade with the Mediterranean world. Large burial mounds and an outer town surround it. It has been called the oldest city north of the Alps.

name: Pompeii
evidenceNote: Pliny the Younger wrote an eyewitness account of the eruption, and thousands of inscriptions and graffiti survive on its walls.
summary: Pompeii was a wealthy Roman town of 10,000 to 20,000 people near Naples. In 79 CE the eruption of Mount Vesuvius buried it, with nearby Herculaneum, under metres of ash and pumice. Because it was sealed so quickly, excavators have found streets, shops, bakeries, houses with wall paintings, and even the shapes of people and animals left as hollows in the ash. Excavations began in the 18th century, and the town gives an unmatched snapshot of everyday Roman life.

name: Acropolis of Athens (Parthenon)
evidenceNote: Athenian inscriptions and ancient writers record its building, as well as excavation and the surviving temples.
summary: The Acropolis is the rocky hill at the centre of Athens. In the 5th century BCE, after the Greeks defeated the Persian invasions, the Athenians rebuilt it with marble temples. The Parthenon, a temple to the goddess Athena, was begun in 447 BCE and finished in 438 BCE, with its sculptures completed by 432 BCE. It also served as a treasury. Later it became a church and then a mosque, until a Venetian bomb exploded gunpowder stored inside in 1687.

image.caption: The Parthenon on the Acropolis of Athens

name: Tollund Man (find site)
evidenceNote: No writing existed in Iron Age Denmark; the body was found in 1950 and dated by radiocarbon.
summary: In 1950 peat cutters near Silkeborg in Denmark found a man's body so well preserved that they thought he was a recent murder victim. He had died between about 405 and 384 BCE, in the Pre-Roman Iron Age. The acid, oxygen-poor bog had preserved his skin and face. A rope around his neck shows he was hanged, but nobody knows whether he was sacrificed or executed. He is one of the best known of northern Europe's many bog bodies.

name: Sarmizegetusa Regia
evidenceNote: Roman writers describe the Dacian wars, and a vessel found here carries the name of King Decebalus.
summary: Sarmizegetusa Regia, high in the Orăștie Mountains of Romania, was the capital and holy centre of the Dacians. King Burebista moved his capital here near the end of his reign in the 1st century BCE, and it reached its height under King Decebalus. Its fortress of stone walls stood beside a sacred area of temples, including a circular sanctuary. The Romans under Emperor Trajan defeated the Dacians in two wars (101–106 CE), took the city, put a garrison in it and tore down much of its fortress.

name: Pont du Gard
dateLabel: 1st century CE; used perhaps until the 6th century
evidenceNote: It is a Roman engineering work dated by archaeology and building style; Roman records of the aqueduct do not give an exact year.
summary: The Pont du Gard is a three-tiered Roman aqueduct bridge over the river Gardon in southern France. Built in the 1st century CE, it carried water about 50 kilometres to the Roman city of Nemausus (Nîmes). The whole channel drops only a tiny amount over its length, showing how precisely Roman engineers worked. It may have carried water until the 6th century, but it was poorly maintained after the 4th. It is one of the best-preserved Roman aqueduct bridges.

image.caption: The Pont du Gard over the river Gardon

name: Colosseum
evidenceNote: Roman writers and inscriptions record its building and the shows held in it.
summary: The Colosseum in Rome is the largest amphitheatre ever built. Emperor Vespasian began it around 72 CE and his son Titus opened it in 80 CE. Built of travertine stone, concrete and tuff, it could hold an estimated 50,000 to 80,000 spectators, who watched gladiator fights, animal hunts and public executions. Gladiator fights are last mentioned in the 5th century, and animal hunts continued until at least 523 CE. Earthquakes and stone robbers later damaged it, but much still stands.

name: Hadrian's Wall
dateLabel: begun 122 CE; Roman rule ended c. 410 CE
evidenceNote: Roman inscriptions, writing tablets and histories record the wall and its soldiers.
summary: Hadrian's Wall was begun in 122 CE on the orders of Emperor Hadrian. It ran about 117 kilometres across northern England, from the River Tyne to the Solway Firth, marking the northern frontier of Roman Britain. Soldiers lived in large forts, smaller milecastles and turrets along it, and its gates may have been customs posts; when fully manned, it may have held almost 10,000 troops. Roman rule in Britain ended around 410 CE, though some forts stayed in use into the 5th century.

name: Pantheon, Rome
evidenceNote: Roman texts and the inscription on its front record it, although Hadrian copied the older builder Agrippa's name onto it, so its exact date is uncertain.
summary: The Pantheon in Rome is a temple to all the gods, rebuilt under Emperor Hadrian and probably dedicated around 126 CE on the site of an earlier temple by Agrippa. A porch of granite columns leads into a round hall covered by a concrete dome with an open hole, the oculus, at the top. Almost two thousand years later it is still the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome. Since 609 CE it has been a church, which is one reason it survives so well.

name: Theodosian Walls of Constantinople
dateLabel: c. 405–413 CE; defended the city until 1453
evidenceNote: Roman law codes and an inscription found in 1993 record the building of the walls.
summary: The Theodosian Walls protected the land side of Constantinople (today Istanbul), the new capital of the Roman Empire. Building began around 405 CE and was finished in 413 under Emperor Theodosius II. Most scholars think a second, outer wall and a moat were added after an earthquake in 447. They were the last great fortification system of the ancient world. For a thousand years they held off attackers, until the Ottoman Turks took the city in 1453. Long stretches still stand.
